title: Electrical Machines

notes.heading: 1. DC Motor Back-EMF, Torque & Speed Control
notes.proseLatex: In a DC machine with $P$ poles, $Z$ armature conductors, and $A$ parallel paths ($A = P$ for lap winding — high current/low voltage; $A = 2$ for wave winding — high voltage/low current), back-EMF is $E_b = \frac{\Phi Z N P}{60 A} \propto \Phi N$. Terminal KVL in a motor reads $V = E_b + I_a R_a$ (whereas in a generator $E_g = V + I_a R_a$!), making $E_b$ self-regulating ($I_a = \frac{V - E_b}{R_a}$; at startup $N=0 \implies E_b=0$, requiring a 3-point/4-point starter!). Electromagnetic torque is $T_a = \frac{E_b I_a}{\omega} \propto \Phi I_a$, and speed obeys $N \propto \frac{V - I_a R_a}{\Phi}$.

keyFormulas.label: DC Motor Back-EMF, Armature Torque & Speed Law
keyFormulas.latex: $E_b = \frac{\Phi Z N P}{60 A},\qquad V = E_b + I_a R_a,\qquad T_a \propto \Phi I_a,\qquad N \propto \frac{V - I_a R_a}{\Phi}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Solve DC shunt/series motor speed, torque, and starter current questions.

examples.problemLatex: A $220\text{ V}$ DC shunt motor ($R_a = 0.5\,\Omega$) draws $I_a = 20\text{ A}$ at $1000\text{ rpm}$. If armature current doubles to $40\text{ A}$ at constant flux, find the new speed.

notes.heading: 2. DC Shunt vs DC Series Motor Characteristics
notes.proseLatex: A DC SHUNT motor has nearly constant $\Phi$, giving linear $T_a \propto I_a$ and flat quasi-constant speed (lathes, machine tools); weakening field flux ($\Phi \downarrow$) speeds it UP above base speed (flux loss causes dangerous overspeed!). A DC SERIES motor carries $I_f = I_a$, so before core saturation $\Phi \propto I_a \implies T_a \propto I_a^2$ (huge starting torque — electric traction, cranes, hoists!), and MUST NEVER be started at no-load because $I_a \to 0 \implies \Phi \to 0 \implies N \to \infty$ (runaway!).

keyFormulas.label: Shunt vs Unsaturation Series Torque Scaling
keyFormulas.latex: $T_{\text{shunt}} \propto I_a;\qquad T_{\text{series, unsat}} \propto I_a^2\;\text{(high starting torque; NEVER run no-load!)}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Select DC series vs shunt motors for traction vs constant-speed drives.

notes.heading: 3. Synchronous Speed, Slip, Rotor Frequency & 1-φ Capacitor Start
notes.proseLatex: An AC stator winding of $P$ poles excited at $f\text{ Hz}$ sets up synchronous speed $N_s = \frac{120 f}{P}\text{ rpm}$. An induction motor runs asynchronously at $N < N_s$ with fractional slip $s = \frac{N_s - N}{N_s}$ ($s=1$ at standstill, $s \approx 0.02\text{--}0.05$ at full load) and rotor current frequency $f_r = s f$! A pure single-phase winding creates only a pulsating (non-rotating) field ($T_{\text{start}} = 0$ — NOT self-starting!), so ceiling fans and pumps add an auxiliary winding + phase-splitting capacitor to create two quadrature fields.

keyFormulas.label: Synchronous Speed, Slip & Rotor Frequency
keyFormulas.latex: $N_s = \frac{120 f}{P},\qquad s = \frac{N_s - N}{N_s},\qquad f_r = s\,f,\qquad P_{\text{ag}}:P_{\text{rcu}}:P_m = 1 : s : (1 - s)$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compute Ns, slip, rotor frequency fr = sf, and air-gap power split.

examples.problemLatex: A $4$-pole, $50\text{ Hz}$ induction motor runs at $1440\text{ rpm}$. Find percentage slip $s$ and rotor current frequency $f_r$.

wbjeebTraps: Single-phase induction motor has ZERO starting torque without an auxiliary phase-splitting winding/capacitor!
NEVER start a DC series motor without mechanical load — $\Phi \propto I_a \to 0$ causes destructive runaway speed.
At standstill (blocked rotor), slip $s = 1$ so $f_r = f$; near synchronous speed, $f_r = sf$ is only $1\text{--}3\text{ Hz}$ (NOT $50\text{ Hz}$!).
